title: Buffett on buybacks
lede: Buffett spent the 1970s hunting for companies that bought back their own shares, because a repurchase below intrinsic value hands continuing owners a free gain. As buybacks became fashionable the argument stayed the same but the language sharpened: the test is price, funds must be surplus, shareholders must be told enough to value the business, and overpaying is simply stupid.

entries.excerpt: The reasoning is simple: if a fine business is selling in the market place for far less than intrinsic value, what more certain or more profitable utilization of capital can there be than significant enlargement of the interests of all owners at that bargain price?
entries.note: The founding case: a discount to intrinsic value is the whole justification, framed as a use of retained earnings.

entries.excerpt: Repurchases of this kind are damage-repair moves. Regular readers will correctly guess that we much prefer repurchases that directly enhance the wealth of owners instead of repurchases that merely repair previous damage. Scoring touchdowns is more exhilarating than recovering one’s fumbles.
entries.note: Distinguishes value-creating buybacks from buybacks that merely undo a share-funded acquisition.

entries.excerpt: When companies with outstanding businesses and comfortable financial positions find their shares selling far below intrinsic value in the marketplace, no alternative action can benefit shareholders as surely as repurchases.
entries.note: The test in embryo: a strong business, spare financial capacity, and a price well below value.

entries.excerpt: Thus, we experienced a triple dip: the company’s business value soared upward, per-share business value increased considerably faster because of stock repurchases and, with a narrowing of the discount, the stock price outpaced the gain in per-share business value.
entries.note: The Washington Post as worked example: cheap repurchases compound per-share value on top of business growth.

entries.excerpt: When managers are making capital allocation decisions - including decisions to repurchase shares - it's vital that they act in ways that increase per-share intrinsic value and avoid moves that decrease it. This principle may seem obvious but we constantly see it violated.
entries.note: The yardstick becomes per-share intrinsic value, and buybacks are folded into capital allocation generally.

entries.excerpt: The benefits that these programs supply us grow as prices fall: When stock prices are low, the funds that an investee spends on repurchases increase our ownership of that company by a greater amount than is the case when prices are higher.
entries.note: The investor's angle: an investee's buyback is worth more to continuing owners the lower the price.

entries.excerpt: That day is past. Now, repurchases are all the rage, but are all too often made for an unstated and, in our view, ignoble reason: to pump or support the stock price.
entries.note: The pivot: from urging buybacks to warning against them, as motive shifts from value to price support.

entries.excerpt: Charlie and I favor repurchases when two conditions are met: first, a company has ample funds to take care of the operational and liquidity needs of its business; second, its stock is selling at a material discount to the company’s intrinsic business value, conservatively calculated.
entries.note: The test stated formally as two conditions, written the year Berkshire began buying its own shares.

entries.excerpt: But never forget: In repurchase decisions, price is all-important. Value is destroyed when purchases are made above intrinsic value. The directors and I believe that continuing shareholders are benefitted in a meaningful way by purchases up to our 120% limit.
entries.note: The test becomes a published ceiling, raised from 110% to 120% of book value.

entries.excerpt: It is puzzling, therefore, that corporate repurchase announcements almost never refer to a price above which repurchases will be eschewed. That certainly wouldn’t be the case if a management was buying an outside business. There, price would always factor into a buy-or-pass decision.
entries.note: Turns the test on other boards: a buyback announcement without a price limit is an unexamined acquisition.

entries.excerpt: When a company says that it contemplates repurchases, it’s vital that all shareholder-partners be given the information they need to make an intelligent estimate of value. Providing that information is what Charlie and I try to do in this report.
entries.note: A third condition made explicit: disclosure, so sellers are not bought out uninformed.

entries.excerpt: Calculations of intrinsic value are far from precise. Consequently, neither of us feels any urgency to buy an estimated $1 of value for a very real 95 cents.
entries.note: The margin of safety widens: a small discount no longer clears the bar.

entries.excerpt: In no way do we think that Berkshire shares should be repurchased at simply any price. I emphasize that point because American CEOs have an embarrassing record of devoting more company funds to repurchases when prices have risen than when they have tanked. Our approach is exactly the reverse.
entries.note: After a record year of buying, the rebuke hardens: most buybacks are pro-cyclical, Berkshire's counter-cyclical.

entries.excerpt: Just as surely, when a company overpays for repurchases, the continuing shareholders lose. At such times, gains flow only to the selling shareholders and to the friendly, but expensive, investment banker who recommended the foolish purchases.
entries.note: Names who wins when the test is failed: leavers and advisers, never those who stay.

entries.excerpt: To this obvious but often overlooked truth, I add my usual caveat: All stock repurchases should be price-dependent. What is sensible at a discount to business-value becomes stupid if done at a premium.
entries.note: Forty years on, the test has become a one-line ritual repeated for every new cohort of readers.

entries.excerpt: We will buy back Berkshire shares when they trade below our estimate of intrinsic value, conservatively determined, ensuring that repurchases enhance per-share value for continuing owners.
entries.note: Greg Abel, not Buffett: the successor restates the test unchanged in his first letter.
